title: Impact of contour on aesthetic judgments and approach-avoidance decisions in architecture
research_question: How does systematic variation in architectural contour (curvilinear vs. rectilinear) impact aesthetic judgments and approach-avoidance decisions, and what are the underlying neural mechanisms?

participants.description: 12 females, 6 males; mean age 23.39 years (SD 4.49); neurologically healthy; normal or corrected-to-normal vision; right-handed (M=74.72, SD=19.29 on standard questionnaire).
participants.recruitment: Recruited under the guidance of The Universidad de la Laguna REB board-El Comité de Ética de la Investigación y de Bienestar Animal (CEIBA).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 200 photographs of architectural spaces (100 rectilinear, 100 curvilinear). Balanced for ceiling height (high/low) and openness (open/closed) within each contour type (25 images per subcategory).

Self-report: 5-point scale 'very unpleasant' to 'very pleasant' (outside fMRI)

mechanisms: Emotion and reward processing: Curvilinear forms elicit pleasant emotions and activate the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), a region involved in reward and emotional salience, suggesting an emotional and reward-based underpinning for aesthetic preference.
Processing fluency/gist perception: Curvilinear forms may be processed more fluently or elicit a more positive gist, influencing aesthetic judgments.

Contextual modulation of threat signals: Rectilinear forms, despite being sharp, may not activate threat-related regions (e.g., amygdala) in architectural contexts due to extensive daily exposure and habituation, or longer stimulus presentation times allowing for cognitive override.

Visual processing for action: Curvilinear spaces activate visual cortex regions (lingual gyrus, calcarine) during approach-avoidance decisions, suggesting differential visual processing related to potential movement or navigation.
Valence dimension of affect: Pleasantness strongly predicts beauty judgments and approach-avoidance decisions, indicating a fundamental role of basic affective valence in these responses.
moderators: Context (e.g., positive vs. negative emotional context for curved objects, built environments vs. landscapes)
Exposure duration (e.g., brief vs. long stimulus presentation for amygdala activation)
implementation_implications: Architectural design should consider contour to enhance aesthetic appeal, as curvilinear forms are consistently preferred as more beautiful.
The emotional impact of architectural features, particularly contour, is significant and should be leveraged to create more pleasant and rewarding spaces.
Further research is needed to understand how specific architectural features influence health and well-being, potentially optimizing design for improved outcomes.

limitations: The study's design might not definitively determine the degree of overlap between neural bases for beauty judgments and approach-avoidance decisions.
The context of built environments might not be comparable to landscapes in terms of promoting evaluation for biological survival, potentially influencing approach-avoidance decisions differently.
Daily exposure to rectilinear spaces might have conditioned participants, reducing the threat signal of sharp contours.
Longer stimulus presentation times (3,000 ms) might have triggered additional cognitive processing that depressed initial, rapid amygdala responses to fearful stimuli.
Amygdala exhibits nonlinear response profiles to facial beauty, suggesting that its response to architectural contour might also be nonlinear, requiring further investigation.
